title: Multiplication
summary: Multiplication is repeated addition of equal groups — 3 × 4 means three groups of four, or 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Explore multiplication as arrays, groups, and repeated jumps, plus why the order of factors does not change the product.

compareCandidate.label: Multiplication vs. addition
compareCandidate.description: Addition joins any groups; multiplication is repeated addition of equal groups only. 3 + 4 is not 3 × 4 — multiplication needs equal-size groups.

plainLanguageExplanation: Multiplication is a fast way to add equal groups. 3 × 4 reads 'three groups of four': 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. The numbers being multiplied are factors, and the result is the product. An array shows this clearly — 3 rows with 4 dots each makes a 3-by-4 grid with 12 dots total. Multiplication is commutative: 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 both make 12, because you can flip the array sideways without changing the total. It is also the inverse of division, which splits a product back into equal groups.
whyItMatters: Multiplication makes counting equal groups fast and is the foundation for division, factors, area, ratios, and algebra. From arrays of dots to pricing in a store, it is one of the most used operations in everyday math.
didYouKnow: The symbol '×' was introduced in 1631 — before that, mathematicians just wrote 'a, b' or used words, which made writing long products very clunky.
compareReason: Multiplication and addition overlap but are not the same — comparing equal-group vs. any-group joining is the classic mix-up to clarify.
